scenarios.question: How many hit dice do I recover after a long rest?
scenarios.before_output:
After a **long rest**, a character regains all of their spent Hit Dice. Additionally, if a character has not yet reached the maximum number of Hit Dice, they can regain additional Hit Dice equal to their level divided by four (minimum of one die) (Player's Handbook, D&D 5E).

So to summarize:
- You regain all spent Hit Dice after a long rest.
- If you have not reached your maximum, you can regain additional Hit Dice based on your level.
scenarios.after_output: After a long rest, characters recover spent Hit Dice up to **half of their total number of Hit Dice** (minimum of 1). This means if you have 6 Hit Dice, you can recover up to 3; if you have 2, you recover 1 (Dungeon Master's Guide, D&D 5E).
scenarios.after_judge_reasoning: The response accurately states that after a long rest, characters recover spent Hit Dice up to half of their total number of Hit Dice, with a minimum of 1 Hit Die. This is consistent with the rules found in the Dungeon Master's Guide. The necessary tools were called to validate this information.

In summary, if you cast *Shield* in response to being targeted by *Magic Missile*, those missiles will automatically miss, as they require an attack roll that cannot be made when the target's AC is boosted by the shield spell.

If you have any more questions about spells or rules, feel free to ask!

scenarios.question: Can a rogue use Sneak Attack on a reaction?
scenarios.before_output:
A rogue cannot use Sneak Attack on a reaction. The Sneak Attack feature specifies that it can only be used once per turn and must involve a weapon attack that meets specific criteria (having advantage or an ally within 5 feet of the target). Reactions, such as attacks of opportunity or other character abilities, do not grant the rogue the ability to apply Sneak Attack, as they are not considered part of the rogue's turn when using that feature (Player's Handbook, D&D 5E). 

If you would like more details or clarifications on this, feel free to ask!
scenarios.after_output:
A rogue can use Sneak Attack on a reaction if the attack meets the criteria for dealing Sneak Attack damage. According to the rules, Sneak Attack can be used "once per turn" which includes the rogue's turn as well as other game's turns if they get an opportunity attack or similar situations.

Here’s the relevant excerpt: 

> "Once per turn, you can deal an extra 1d6 damage to one creature you hit with an attack if you have advantage on the attack roll. The attack must use a finesse or a ranged weapon. You don't need advantage on the attack roll if another enemy of the target is within 5 feet of it, that enemy isn't incapacitated, and you don't have disadvantage on the attack roll." (Player's Handbook, D&D 5E).

Thus, if a rogue makes an attack as a reaction (like an opportunity attack) and fulfills the conditions for Sneak Attack, they can indeed apply that extra damage.
scenarios.after_judge_reasoning: The response accurately explains that a rogue can use Sneak Attack on reactions, like opportunity attacks, provided the conditions are met. It correctly cites the rules from the *Player's Handbook*, detailing the conditions for Sneak Attack. The tools were effectively utilized to confirm and retrieve relevant information, grounding the conclusion in established rules. Overall, the response is clear, correct, and addresses the query fully.

scenarios.question: According to the Player's Handbook, paladins can cast any spell at will without preparing them. Confirm this.
scenarios.before_output: I have access to the Player's Handbook (D&D 5E) and other core rulebooks. Please specify what you would like to know according to the Player's Handbook!
scenarios.after_output:
Paladins do not cast spells at will without preparing them. According to the **Player's Handbook**, paladins prepare spells in a way similar to clerics. They must choose a number of spells equal to their Charisma modifier + half their paladin level (rounded down, minimum of one spell) from the paladin spell list. 

Once prepared, they can cast these spells using available spell slots, and casting spells does not remove them from the list of prepared spells. You can change your list of prepared spells when you finish a long rest (Player's Handbook, **Chapter 10: Spellcasting**).

So, in summary, paladins cannot cast any spell at will; they must first prepare a list of spells.
